claim: The forests of eastern Asia (EA) and eastern North America (ENA) share 65 genera of seed plants with closely related species occurring in the two areas.
source: The forests of eastern Asia (EA) and eastern North America (ENA) share 65 genera of seed plants with closely related species occurring in the two areas (Li, 1952; Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wu, 1983; Wen, 1999; Wen et al., 2010; Wen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature documenting the EA-ENA floristic disjunction.

claim: The EA-ENA floristic disjunction is a major phytogeographic pattern of the Northern Hemisphere and has been known since the time of Linnaeus.
source: This well-known floristic disjunction is a major phytogeographic pattern of the Northern Hemisphere and has been known since the time of Linnaeus (Wen, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents established knowledge in biogeography.

claim: The divergence times of disjunct sister species in EA and ENA varied greatly from the Miocene to the Pleistocene or even more recently (15 mya to <2.0 mya).
source: Previous analyses using mainly plastid and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) DNA sequence markers revealed that the divergence times of disjunct sister species in EA and ENA varied greatly from the Miocene to the Pleistocene or even more recently (15 mya to <2.0 mya), although some disjunct clades in the two areas diverged earlier (Xiang et al., 2000; Wen, 2001; Milne and Abbott, 2002; Donoghue and Smith, 2004; Harris et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies that estimated divergence times.

claim: In each of the 20 taxon pairs, more than 90% of POGs are under purifying selection.
source: In all pairs, the ratios at peak frequencies are highly similar and more than 90% of the genes are overall under purifying selection (referred to as purifying selection in short) based on their average Ka/Ks ratios < 0.9 across all sites within the genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Ka/Ks ratio data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Less than 10% of POGs are under positive selection in each taxon pair.
source: another small proportion, from 3.1% (in Gelsemium) to 8.8% (in Nelumbo), is under putative positive selection based on values of Ka/Ks ratios greater than 1.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Ka/Ks ratio data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A very small proportion of POGs (0.6% to 2.0%) is under putative strong positive selection with Ka/Ks ratios ranging from 2 to 7 and rarely to 17.
source: A very small proportion, from 0.6% (in Gelsemium) to 2.0% (in Nelumbo), is under putative strong positive selection with Ka/Ks ratios ranging from 2 to 7 and rarely to 17 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data and Figure 3 showing the distribution of Ka/Ks values.

claim: Fourteen GO terms annotated to biological processes responding to various stimuli are shared by 10-15 taxon pairs.
source: Among these, 12 were shared by 10–15 taxon pairs. These 12 genes were annotated to the nucleus, protein complex, hydrolase activity, zinc ion binding, RNA binding, ATP binding, structural constituent of ribosome, oxidoreductase activity, cellular protein modification process, translation, single-organism biosynthetic process, and oxidation-reduction process (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results presented in the manuscript and supplementary files.

claim: One GO term (integral component of membrane) is shared by all 20 taxon pairs.
source: A single GO term is shared by all 20 taxon pairs and is annotated to integral component of membrane (ICM) in the CC category (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results.

claim: Species divergence times are positively correlated with abundance of POGs under moderate purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks < 0.5).
source: The divergence times of taxon pairs are also positively correlated with the abundance of genes under moderate purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks <0.5; r = 0.73; p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of divergence time and Ka/Ks data.

claim: Species divergence times are negatively correlated with abundance of POGs under strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks < 0.1).
source: negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks <0.1; r = - 0.64; p<0.009; Figure 5; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of divergence time and Ka/Ks data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The number of POGs in the leaf transcriptomes of the 20 biogeographic taxon pairs varies from 8596 to 15161.
source: The number of POGs in the leaf transcriptomes of the 20 biogeographic taxon pairs varies from 8596 to 15161 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Among the POGs, 2241 are shared by over 50% of the taxa.
source: Among these POGs, 2241 are shared by over 50% of the taxa, 333 are shared by over 80% of the taxa, 79 are shared by over 90% of the taxa, and seven are shared by all of the taxa.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of shared POGs across taxa.

claim: Most POGs exhibit low divergence, with synonymous substitution (Ks) values less than 0.1 and nonsynonymous substitution values (Ka) less than 0.04.
source: Most of these genes exhibit low divergence, with synonymous substitution (Ks) values less than 0.1 and nonsynonymous substitution values (Ka) less than 0.04.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks and Ka values calculated for POGs.

claim: Less than 1% of the genes exhibit greater divergence with Ks values greater than 0.15 and Ka values greater than 0.05.
source: Less than 1% of the genes exhibit greater divergence with Ks values greater than 0.15 (Figure 1) and Ka values greater than 0.05 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks and Ka data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The Ks values at peak frequency range among the taxon pairs from <0.01 to <0.06.
source: The Ks values at peak frequency when plotted in intervals of 0.01 range among the taxon pairs from <0.01 to<0.06 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks distribution data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In Convallaria, Liriodendron, Cotinus, Menispermum, and Campsis, the Ks values at peak frequency are less than 0.01.
source: In Convallaria, Liriodendron, Cotinus, Menispermum, and Campsis, the Ks values at peak frequency are less than 0.01
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks data for specific genera.

claim: In Cornus-2, Dysosma, Nelumbo, Penthorum, and Sassafras, the Ks values at peak frequency are between 0.01 and 0.02.
source: while in Cornus-2, Dysosma, Nelumbo, Penthorum, and Sassafras, they are between 0.01 and 0.02.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks data for specific genera.

claim: The largest Ks values at peak frequency are observed in Acorus and Gelsemium, between 0.05 and 0.06.
source: The largest values are observed in Acorus and Gelsemium, between 0.05 and 0.06 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ks data for specific genera.

claim: A portion of the POGs (53-237 among the genera) were aligned to putative single-copy or low-copy genes shared by seed plants.
source: A portion of the POGs, 53–237 among the genera, were aligned to putative single-copy or low-copy genes shared by seed plants (Li et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by mapping analysis results comparing POGs to known single-copy genes.

claim: 75-365 POGs were mapped to strict single-copy genes shared by 20 angiosperm genomes.
source: and 75–365 were mapped to strict single-copy genes shared by 20 angiosperm genomes (De Smet et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by mapping analysis results.

claim: Nelumbo has 87.6% of the genes with Ka/Ks ratios < 0.9.
source: The exception was Nelumbo, which has 87.6% of the genes with Ka/Ks ratios < 0.9.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data for Nelumbo.

claim: Gelsemium has the greatest proportion of genes under purifying selection with 94.9% of the genes with Ka/Ks ratios < 0.9.
source: The greatest proportion of genes under purifying selection was observed in Gelsemium, which had 94.9% of the genes with Ka/Ks ratios < 0.9.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data for Gelsemium.

claim: A very small proportion of POGs (1.6% in Acorus to 3.7% in Nelumbo) is evolving nearly neutrally with Ka/Ks ratios in the range of 0.9-1.1.
source: A very small proportion, from 1.6% (in Acorus) to 3.7% (in Nelumbo), is evolving nearly neutrally with Ka/Ks ratios in the range of 0.9–1.1
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data.

claim: Among the taxon pairs, 41% (in Convallaria) to 68% (in Gelsemium) of the POGs fall into the category of moderate purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks < 0.5).
source: Among the taxon pairs, we observed 41% (in Convallaria) to 68% (in Gelsemium) of the POGs fall into the category of moderate purifying selection
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data categorized by selection intensity.

claim: 11% (in Gelsemium) to 36% (in Convallaria) of POGs fall into the category of strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks < 0.1).
source: 11% (in Gelsemium) to 36% (in Convallaria) fall into the category of strong purifying selection
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data categorized by selection intensity.

claim: 9.7% (in Acorus) to 19.5% (in Nelumbo) of POGs fall into the category of relaxed purifying selection (0.5 < Ka/Ks < 0.9).
source: while 9.7% (in Acorus) to 19.5% (in Nelumbo) fall into the category of relaxed purifying selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ka/Ks ratio data categorized by selection intensity.

claim: In all taxon pairs, the relative abundance of POGs under different categories of selection pressures follows the same order: moderate purifying selection > strong purifying selection > relaxed purifying selection > weak/moderate positive selection > putatively neutral > strong positive selection.
source: In all taxon pairs, the relative abundance of POGs under the different categories of selection pressures follows the same order, from high to low, as moderate purifying selection, strong purifying selection, relaxed purifying selection, weak/moderate positive selection, putatively neutral, and strong positive selection (Figure 4; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses using the seven POGs shared by all taxa recovered relationships congruent with the APG IV summary phylogeny and classification.
source: The results recovered the relationships of the 20 lineages congruent with the APG IV summary phylogeny and classification (The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, 2016) (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The estimated divergence times suggest that isolation of the species pairs occurred in an interval between the late Miocene and Pleistocene (~10.67 –~1.69 mya).
source: The estimated divergence times suggested that isolation of the species pairs occurred in an interval between the late Miocene and Pleistocene (~10.67 –~1.69 mya; Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by divergence time estimation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Species divergence time is positively correlated with the Ks value at peak frequency across taxon pairs (r = 0.8034; p<0.001).
source: Species divergence time was positively correlated with the Ks value at peak frequency across taxon pairs (Figure 5; r = 0.8034; p<0.001; for values used for the correlation analysis, see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Ks values at peak frequency are positively correlated with the abundance of genes under moderate purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks <0.5; r = 0.9324; p<0.001).
source: the Ks values at peak frequency of the taxon pairs are: (1) positively correlated with the abundance of genes under moderate purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks <0.5; r = 0.9324; p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of Ks and gene abundance data.

claim: The Ks values at peak frequency are negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under putative positive selection (Ka/Ks >=1.0, r = -0.5344; p=0.015).
source: (2) negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under putative positive selection (Ka/Ks >=1.0, r = - 0.5344; p=0.015; 1.1 <= Ka/Ks <2, r = - 0.62; p=0.004)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of Ks and gene abundance data.

claim: The Ks values at peak frequency are negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under putative strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks <0.1; r = -0.7940; p<0.001).
source: and (3) negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under putative strong purifying selection (Ka/Ks <0.1; r = - 0.7940; p<0.001) (Figure 6; Supplementary file 3, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The number of genes under strong positive selection (Ka/Ks >2) varies among the taxon pairs from 72 (in Campsis) to 184 (in Nelumbo).
source: The number of genes under strong positive selection (Ka/Ks >2) varies among the taxon pairs from 72 (in Campsis) to 184 (in Nelumbo) (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 2.

claim: In each taxon pair, approximately half of the genes under strong positive selection have GO annotations.
source: In each pair, approximately half of these genes have GO annotations (Table 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation results shown in Table 2.

claim: The GO annotations of genes under strong positive selection mapped to a total of 223 GO terms, varying from 21 (in Cornus-2) to 46 (in Convallaria) in each taxon pair.
source: that, in combination among all pairs, mapped to a total of 223 GO terms, varying from 21 (in Cornus-2) to 46 (in Convallaria) in each taxon pair (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results.

claim: 44.8% (100/223) of the GO terms are unique to a single lineage.
source: Many of these GO terms are unique to a single lineage (100/223 = 44.8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results.

claim: A majority (59) of the lineage-specific GO terms belongs to the Biological Process (BP) categorization.
source: A majority (59) of these lineage-specific GO terms belongs to the Biological Process (BP) categorization, while 23 belong to the Molecular Function (MF) ontology, and 16 belong to the Cell Components (CC) ontology (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation categorization results.

claim: Fourteen of the BP GO terms were annotated to responses to various stimuli and were distributed among 11 taxon pairs.
source: Fourteen of the BP GO terms were annotated to responses to various stimuli (biotic or abiotic, external or internal stimuli), defense response, immune process, or signal transduction and were distributed among 11 taxon pairs, with each term was present in 1–3 pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results.

claim: 124 of the 223 GO terms (55.2%) are shared by two or more of the 20 taxon pairs.
source: In all, 124 of the 223 GO terms (55.2%) are shared by two or more of the 20 taxon pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis results.

claim: Within the CC category, all pairs have the greatest proportion annotated to integral component of membrane (ICM).
source: However, within the CC category, all pairs have the greatest proportion annotated to ICM (Figure 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Most genes with Ka/Ks > 2 (>57% in all taxon pairs, >70% in 15 pairs) were also under positive selection according to the variation cluster method.
source: The analysis of the Ka/Ks > 2 genes using the variation cluster method (Wagner, 2007) showed most of them (>57% in all taxon pairs, >70% in 15 pairs) were also under positive selection (indicated by significant p value for test of clustered nucleotide substitutions) (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by variation cluster analysis results.

claim: The molecular divergence in the POGs is generally low after geographic speciation.
source: The pattern we observed indicates that in each of the taxon pair, including the 16 EA-ENA pairs, most of the genes show shallow divergence or evolve slowly at a similar rate, while a small proportion of the genes evolve faster. This suggests that the molecular divergence in the POGs is generally low after geographic speciation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed patterns of Ks, Ka, and Ka/Ks values.

claim: The peak frequency range of Ks, Ka, and Ka/Ks values revealed substantial differences in the magnitudes among genera, indicating that the taxon pairs have diverged to different extents.
source: The peak frequency range of Ks, Ka, and Ka/Ks values revealed substantial differences in the magnitudes among genera, indicating that the taxon pairs have diverged to different extents, likely reflecting their relative timing of divergence and/or varying selection pressures among different genera.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the variation in peak frequency values across genera.

claim: The major pattern of divergence revealed by analyses of many nuclear genes for the 16 EA-ENA disjunct taxon pairs is consistent with previous studies based on ITS and/or a few plastid gene sequences.
source: The major pattern of divergence revealed here by analyses of many nuclear genes for the 16 EA-ENA disjunct taxon pairs is consistent with the previous mega-synthesis of studies of individual lineages that were largely based on ITS and/or a few plastid gene sequences or non-coding markers (Donoghue and Smith, 2004; Wen et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim compares current results with previous studies cited in the text.

claim: The divergence times estimated for the EA-NA disjunct pairs support the importance of a geographical connection through the Bering Land Bridge (BLB) and perhaps also long-distance dispersal (LDD) to explain a part of the EA-ENA floristic similarity.
source: The divergence times estimated for the EA-NA (ENA, WNA, or NA) disjunct pairs in this study support the importance of a geographical connection through the Bering Land Bridge (BLB) and perhaps also long-distance dispersal (LDD) to explain a part of the EA-ENA floristic similarity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the divergence time estimates and geological evidence about the BLB.

claim: The Bering Land Bridge was available as a floristic connection throughout most of the Paleogene and Neogene and closed for the potential migration of terrestrial organisms between 7.4 and 4.8 mya.
source: Geological evidence indicates that the BLB was available as a floristic connection throughout most of the Paleogene and Neogene and closed for the potential migration of terrestrial organisms between 7.4 and 4.8 mya (Marincovich and Gladenkov, 1999; Graham, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to geological studies.

claim: The North Atlantic Land Bridge (NALB) broke up in the early Eocene.
source: while the North Atlantic Land Bridge (NALB) broke up in the early Eocene (Marincovich et al., 1990; Tiffney, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to geological studies.

claim: A repeated pattern of divergence of POGs is observed among the taxon pairs in allopatric speciation.
source: Our analyses also revealed a repeated pattern of divergence of POGs among the taxon pairs in allopatric speciation. That is, we observed the same order of relative abundance of POGs under various selection pressures (Figure 4), disregarding the relative timing of species isolation
evidence: This claim is supported by the consistent pattern shown in Figure 4 across all taxon pairs.

claim: Most of the molecular evolution (or DNA substitution) in the POGs was neutral (or synonymous).
source: The observed pattern further suggests that most of the molecular evolution (or DNA substitution) in the POGs was neutral (or synonymous).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that most POGs are under purifying selection with excess synonymous substitutions.

claim: The deciduous forests in eastern Asia and eastern North America are situated at similar latitudes and may have similar regional climatic and ecological conditions.
source: The deciduous forests in eastern Asia and eastern North America are situated at similar latitudes, and both China and the United States have an eastern coast line; thus, they may have similar regional climatic and ecological conditions (E. Ricklefs et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about the geographic and climatic similarities.

claim: There are presumably low divergence pressures for gene functional evolution in eastern Asia and eastern North America.
source: Therefore, there are presumably low divergence pressures for gene functional evolution in the two areas.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar climatic and ecological conditions between EA and ENA.

claim: Most genes are expected to evolve slowly under purifying selection to conserve ancestral functions.
source: One would therefore expect most genes to evolve slowly under purifying selection to conserve ancestral functions and the observed excess synonymous substitutions (in comparison to non-synonymou substitutions) in these genes were results of elimination of nonsynonymous substitutions by natural selection while the neutral synonymous substitutions were fixed by genetic drift.
evidence: This claim represents a theoretical expectation based on evolutionary theory.

claim: Differences in micro-abiotic and biotic environments between eastern Asia and eastern North America could have driven diversifying evolution of some genes for local adaptation, speciation, and subsequent divergence.
source: On the other hand, although eastern Asia and eastern North America share similarities in general climate, there must be differences in micro-abiotic and biotic environments between the two regions which could have driven diversifying evolution of some genes in the sister lineages for local adaptation, speciation, and subsequent divergence.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis inferred from the observation of genes under positive selection and environmental differences.

claim: The conserved order of gene abundance observed in all taxon pairs may be essential to maintaining a balance between the ability to preserve the ancestral biological system and the ability to evolve new features that are beneficial for new adaptation.
source: The conserved order of gene abundance, as observed in all taxon pairs in this study, may be essential to maintaining a balance between the ability to preserve the ancestral biological system and the ability to evolve new features that are beneficial for new adaptation.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis inferred from the observed pattern of gene abundance.

claim: The repeated pattern of variation of relative abundance of POGs under different selection pressures among taxa may represent a genomic 'rule' for allopatric speciation.
source: The repeated pattern of variation of relative abundance of POGs under different selection pressures among taxa may represent a genomic 'rule' that can be tested by examining all gene families in the transcriptomes or genomes of the studied taxa.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis proposed based on the observed repeated pattern.

claim: Molecular evolution in the allopatric taxa is mostly neutral involving mostly silent nucleotide substitutions in the genome.
source: It is allied with a hypothesis that molecular evolution in the allopatric taxa is mostly neutral involving mostly silent nucleotide substitutions in the genome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observed patterns.

claim: As geographic isolation or divergence proceeded in time, the purifying selection pressures of some genes may have shifted from high intensity during early geographic isolation to lower intensity at the later stage of isolation.
source: Our observation of the length of time of species isolation is positively correlated with the abundance of genes under moderate pressure of purifying selection (0.1 < Ka/Ks < 0.5), but negatively correlated with the abundance of genes under strong pressure of purifying selection (Ka/Ks < 0.1) (Figure 5; Figure 6), suggests that as geographic isolation or divergence proceeded in time (within the time window of divergence of the species pairs studied), the purifying selection pressures of some genes may have shifted from high intensity during early geographic isolation to lower intensity at the later stage of isolation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation patterns observed in the data.

claim: The shift in purifying selection intensity might be attributed to changes of evolutionary trajectories of the gene at some sites where replacement substitutions are favored for modification of the ancestral functions.
source: The shift might be attributed to changes of evolutionary trajectories of the gene at some sites where replacement substitutions are favored for modification of the ancestral functions leading to relevant morphological/ecological divergence between the species pairs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed shift in selection intensity.

claim: A relaxed purifying selection intensity of some genes could be simply a result of accumulation of slightly deleterious nonsynonymous substitutions rather than adaptive evolution.
source: Alternatively, a relaxed purifying selection intensity of some genes could be simply a result of accumulation of slightly deleterious nonsynonymous substitutions rather than adaptive evolution.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed to explain the observed pattern.

claim: As time of isolation proceeded, pressure of positive selection for some genes might have also relaxed to lower Ka/Ks values due to accumulation of mutations at synonymous sites in the genes.
source: An observation of a weak negative relationship between Ks peak values and abundance of genes under positive selection pressure (Ka/Ks > 1; Figure 6) in our study also suggests that as time of isolation proceeded, pressure of positive selection for some genes might have also relaxed to a lower Ka/Ks values due to accumulation of mutations at synonymous sites in the genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed negative correlation.

claim: Eight of the 79 POGs shared by 90% or more taxa had a correlation between Ka/Ks values and divergence times at r > 0.5.
source: A simple scattered plot in excel for the divergence times and the Ka/Ks values (with Ka/Ks values = 0, 99 removed) of the 79 POGs shared by 90% or more taxa revealed that eight of these genes had a correlation at r > 0.5, among which two correlations were positive and six were negative (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of specific genes.

claim: The Ka/Ks ratios of POGs that showed a correlation with times were all smaller than 1.0 (all <0.5 except for a couple of cases).
source: The Ka/Ks ratios of POGs that showed a correlation with times were all smaller than 1.0 (all <0.5 except for a couple of cases).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of Ka/Ks values in genes showing correlation with time.

claim: Some genes may have shifted the pressure of purifying selection (intensified or relaxed) during the evolutionary divergence of the taxon pair.
source: These data provide another line of indirect evidence congruent with the hypothesis that some genes may have indeed shifted the pressure of purifying selection (intensified or relaxed) during the evolutionary divergence of the taxon pair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation patterns observed in specific genes.

claim: The presence and elimination of slightly deleterious nonsynonymous substitutions play a major role in the changes of Ka/Ks ratios.
source: This observation suggests, perhaps, the presence and elimination of slightly deleterious nonsynonymous substitutions play a major role in the changes of Ka/Ks ratios.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of genes with Ka/Ks < 0.5.

claim: The evolutionary fate of most of the 79 POGs is more taxon-specific independent of time.
source: Lack of correlation between Ka/Ks ratios and time for most of the 79 POGs also suggests that the evolutionary fate of most of these POGs is more taxon-specific independent of time.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of correlation in most genes.

claim: The aquatic eudicot Nelumbo has the largest proportion of its POGs under positive selection and the smallest proportion of POGs under purifying selection among the 20 lineages examined.
source: For example, among the 20 lineages we examined, the aquatic eudicot Nelumbo has the largest proportion of its POGs under positive selection and the smallest proportion of POGs under purifying selection
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Ka/Ks data across all lineages.

claim: The terrestrial twining vine Gelsemium has the smallest proportion of POGs under positive selection and the largest proportion under purifying selection among the 20 lineages examined.
source: while the reverse is found in the terrestrial twining vine Gelsemium, a member of the asterid clade Gentianales.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Ka/Ks data across all lineages.

claim: The two species of Nelumbo differ in four features of their reproductive structures, including tepal color and persistence, receptacle color, and fruit shape.
source: The two species of Nelumbo, N. nucifera (EA) and N. lutea (ENA), differ in four features of their reproductive structures, including tepal color and persistence, receptacle color, and fruit shape.
evidence: This claim represents morphological observations of Nelumbo species.

claim: In Gelsemium, 12 morphological characters in reproductive structures and two vegetative structures differ between the two disjunct species.
source: In Gelsemium, 12 morphological characters in reproductive structures (including inflorescence size, floral shape/size, fruit and seed morphology, etc.; see list in Wyatt et al., 1993) and two vegetative structures (petiole length and leaf shape) differ between the two disjunct species (Wyatt et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study documenting morphological differences.

claim: Possible ecological/environmental pressures or selection agents that differ between the growing habitats of the taxon pairs in EA and ENA or other areas may have driven the extent of divergence in these genera.
source: The GO terms of these genes (Supplementary file 5) support that possible ecological/environmental pressures or selection agents that differ between the growing habitats of the taxon pairs in EA and ENA or other areas may have driven the extent of divergence in these genera.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GO terms associated with positively selected genes.

claim: Positive selection genes (Ka/Ks > 2) with GO terms are enriched for immunity/stimuli responses.
source: For example, the positive selection genes (Ka/Ks > 2) with GO terms in our study are enriched for immunity/stimuli responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO annotation analysis of positively selected genes.

claim: Positive selection genes in mammals are enriched for a wide variety of functions related to immunity and defense.
source: Similar case is also found in positive selection genes in mammals which were enriched for a wide variety of functions related to immunity and defense (Kosiol et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on mammalian genomes.

claim: A potential common regional force acting on the studied taxa resulted in the adaptive evolution of ICM genes.
source: This also suggests that a potential common regional force acting on these taxa resulted in the adaptive evolution of ICM genes, which may be involved in some of the common biological processes, such as signaling associated with host-microbe interactions and responses to various stimuli.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ICM is the only GO term shared by all taxon pairs.

claim: Natural selection tends to target a set of available genes in repeated patterns of genomic divergence associated with species formation.
source: Recent studies have revealed repeated patterns of genomic divergence associated with species formation (Pereira et al., 2016). Such patterns was considered as evidence suggesting that natural selection tends to target a set of available genes (Pereira et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: A set of genes was targeted for strong positive selection in each taxon pair, suggesting that these genes may play a role for the allopatric divergence of the studied taxon pairs.
source: Our study found a set of genes was targeted for strong positive selection in each taxon pair, suggesting that these genes may play a role for the allopatric divergence of the studied taxon pairs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the identification of positively selected genes in each pair.

claim: OrthoMCL is known to perform reasonably well in identifying orthologous genes.
source: OrthoMCL is known to perform reasonably well in identifying orthologous genes (Chen et al., 2007; Altenhoff and Dessimoz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies evaluating OrthoMCL performance.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses of the seven POGs shared among the 20 taxon pairs showed all taxon pairs were grouped as sister taxa in each of the gene trees.
source: We conducted phylogenetic analyses of the seven POGs shared among the 20 taxon pairs and 79 POGs shared by >90% taxon pairs, respectively, using raxml. The results showed all taxon pairs were grouped as sister taxa in each of the gene trees, in accordance with the expectation that the sequence pairs are orthologous genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis results.

claim: Most of the genes (except a few) with Ka/Ks > 2 had Ks > 0.005.
source: In our data, most of the genes (except a few) with Ka/Ks > 2 had Ks > 0.005 (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by examination of Ks values in genes with high Ka/Ks ratios.

claim: The genes with Ka/Ks > 2 have a range of Ks values from small to large in all taxon pairs.
source: Our plots of the Ks vs. Ka/Ks values in each taxon pair show that the genes with Ka/Ks > 2 have a range of Ks values from small to large in all taxon pairs (Appendix 1—figures 3–22)
evidence: This claim is supported by plots shown in Appendix 1 figures 3-22.

claim: The divergence times of each taxon pair calculated using BEAST and the global phylogeny may be somewhat underestimated due to sparse sampling of a deep phylogeny.
source: We also recognize that the divergence times of each taxon pair calculated using BEAST (Drummond and Rambaut, 2007) and the global phylogeny including all 20 pairs may be somewhat underestimated due to sparse sampling of a deep phylogeny containing both very long and short branches and few calibrations only at deep nodes (see Methods and Xiang et al., 2011) that may fall beyond the smoothing capability of BEAST.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a potential limitation in the divergence time estimation method.

claim: The divergence time results are very similar to previous estimates based on rbcL sequences.
source: However, the results are very similar to previous estimates based on rbcL sequences (Xiang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim compares current results with previous estimates.

claim: The relative order of divergence of the species pairs estimated in this study is expected to be consistent despite possible bias in absolute divergence times.
source: Despite the possible bias, the influence may be similar across the tree and does not renter their suitability for correlation analyses conducted in the study because the relative order of divergence of the species pairs estimated here is expected to be consistent.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about the nature of potential bias in divergence time estimation.

claim: The POGs examined in this study represented 52-68% of the total orthologous gene families in the transcriptome data.
source: The POGs examined in this study represented 52–68% of the total orthologous gene families in the transcriptome data (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous nucleotide substitutions (Ka/Ks) is probably the most common measure of selection pressure and for identifying positive selection.
source: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous nucleotide substitutions (Ka/Ks) is probably the most common measure of selection pressure and for identifying positive selection (Ka/Ks > 1) (Yang, 2003) in molecular evolutionary studies.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in molecular evolution supported by citation.

claim: The Ka/Ks method is known to be a conservative approach to call positive selection on a gene as it uses an average Ka/Ks ratio across all nucleotide sites.
source: The method is known to be a conservative approach to call positive selection on a gene as it uses an average Ka/Ks ratio across all nucleotide sites.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the Ka/Ks method.

claim: Uncertainty in Ka/Ks ratios is high when Ks is zero or close to zero.
source: We are aware that uncertainty in Ka/Ks ratios is high when Ks is zero or close to zero.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about limitations of Ka/Ks estimation.

claim: Genes with Ks = 0 and genes with Ka/Ks = 99 were removed for all analyses to minimize problems with uncertainty in Ka/Ks ratios.
source: To minimize this problem, we removed genes with Ks = 0 and genes with Ka/Ks = 99 for all analyses and only focused on genes with Ka/Ks > 2 as candidates of strong positive selection for gene annotation analysis.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision made in the study.

claim: The Ka/Ks > 2 ratios in genes under positive selection are unlikely a result of saturation of synonymous substitutions.
source: Further, the Ka/Ks > 2 ratios in these genes are unlikely a result of saturation of synonymous substitutions. Saturation of synonymous substitutions is often expected at deeper phylogenetic levels.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about when saturation occurs.

claim: Both the Ka/Ks and variation cluster methods may underestimate the number of genes under positive selection.
source: Both the Ka/Ks and variation cluster methods may underestimate the number of genes under positive selection because some genes with Ka/Ks < 1 may be under positive selection at only a few sites and these sites may not be necessarily clustered in the gene.
evidence: This claim represents knowledge about limitations of the methods used.

claim: The genes identified as under positive selection by both Ka/Ks and variation cluster methods are likely the true positive selection genes.
source: The genes identified as under positive selection by both methods are likely the true positive selection genes and will provide top candidates for future studies for their functions in driving allopatric divergence in these taxa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the use of two independent methods.
